What are radical and rational equations?

A radical equation has the unknown under a root, such as x+7=x+1. A rational equation has the unknown in a denominator, such as 3x+1=2x−1. Both are solved by turning them into ordinary polynomial equations: square both sides, or multiply by the denominators. Both steps can introduce extraneous roots, answers that do not satisfy the original equation, so every candidate must be checked.

Try changing the input

Solve x+7=x+1. Squaring gives x=2 or x=−3, but at x=−3 the right side is −2, and a square root is never negative. Only x=2 survives.

What this calculator does

  • Radical mode: solves ax+b=cx+d by squaring, then checks each candidate.
  • Rational mode: solves any equation of fractions with polynomials in x, such as xx−2+1x=2x(x−2). It lists the excluded values, multiplies by the least common denominator, solves, and rejects roots that make a denominator 0.

The graph shows both sides of the equation, with solutions marked and rejected roots flagged.

Why extraneous roots appear

Squaring loses the sign. 2 and −2 have the same square, so u=v and u=−v both become u=v2. The squared equation has the solutions of both, and only those with v≥0 belong to the original.

Multiplying by an expression that can be 0. Multiplying both sides by x−1 is only reversible when x≠1. A root that makes a denominator 0 was never allowed in the original equation.

Graph view

The squared equation describes where the line meets the whole sideways parabola y2=ax+b. The square root is only its upper half, so crossings with the lower half are extraneous.

Variables explained

TermMeaning
a,bThe radicand is ax+b.
c,dThe right side of a radical equation, cx+d.
Excluded valueAn x-value that makes a denominator 0.
LCDLeast common denominator: the smallest expression every denominator divides.
Extraneous rootA solution of the transformed equation that fails the original one.

How the methods work

Radical equations

Isolate the root first. Squaring ax+b=cx+d gives

ax+b=c2x2+2cdx+d2  ⇒  c2x2+(2cd−a)x+(d2−b)=0,

a quadratic (or a linear equation when c=0). Solve it and test each root in the original equation.

Rational equations

Write each side as one fraction, then multiply both sides by the LCD. The fractions clear, leaving a polynomial equation. Solve it and discard any root that is an excluded value.

Complete worked example

Problem

Solve x+7=x+1.

Step 1: Square both sides

x+7=x2+2x+1

Step 2: Solve the quadratic

x2+x−6=0  ⇒  (x+3)(x−2)=0  ⇒  x=−3 or x=2

Step 3: Check

x=2: 9=3 and 2+1=3. ✓

x=−3: 4=2 but −3+1=−2. Rejected.

The solution is x=2.

Second worked example: a rational equation

Problem

Solve xx−1=1x−1+2.

Step 1: Excluded value

The denominator is 0 at x=1, so x≠1.

Step 2: Multiply every term by the LCD, x−1

x=1+2(x−1)  ⇒  x=2x−1  ⇒  x=1

Step 3: Check

x=1 is the excluded value, so it is rejected. The equation has no solution: for every other x the left side is 1+1x−1, which never equals 1x−1+2.

Practical applications

  • Pendulums and free fall: T=2πL/g and t=2h/g are solved for a length or height.
  • Lenses: the thin-lens equation 1f=1do+1di is a rational equation.
  • Resistors in parallel and work rates: 1R=1R1+1R2 has the same form as "two pipes fill a tank".
  • Average speed: trips at different speeds give equations with the unknown in a denominator.

Common mistakes

  1. Squaring term by term. (x+1)2=x2+2x+1, not x2+1.
  2. Squaring before isolating the root. Get the root alone on one side first.
  3. Not checking the answers. Squaring and clearing denominators can both add roots.
  4. Forgetting the excluded values. Write them down before you multiply anything.

Assumptions and limitations

  • Radical mode handles a single square root of a linear expression equal to a linear expression.
  • Rational mode accepts polynomials and whole-number powers in x; after clearing denominators the degree must be at most 8.
  • Rational roots are exact; other roots are found numerically and shown to 6 decimal places.

Frequently asked questions

What is an extraneous solution?

A value that solves the equation after squaring or clearing denominators, but not the original equation.

How do I solve a square root equation?

Isolate the root, square both sides, solve the resulting equation, then substitute each answer into the original equation.

How do I solve an equation with fractions that contain x?

Note the excluded values, multiply every term by the least common denominator, solve, and reject any excluded value.

Can a radical equation have no solution?

Yes. If every candidate is extraneous, as in √(x) = −2, there is no solution.
